fields.label: Panels ×8
rows: Polyisoprene, and the standard silent-block compound. The highest resilience and best fatigue life of the eight, with the lowest dynamic-to-static stiffness ratio — the property that decides whether a bush behaves in service the way it did on the rate curve. Not for oil, fuel or sustained heat.

Ethylene acrylic elastomer. Our signature compound, supplied to Mahindra & Mahindra for engine and transmission applications, and the reason this category exists in its current form. Holds its properties where oil, heat and ozone act together — the condition under a bonnet, and the one that ends a natural rubber bush.

Nitrile butadiene rubber, the general-purpose industry standard. Outstanding resistance to petroleum oils and hydraulic fluids at moderate temperature — the choice for a mounting that sits in oil. Dynamic behaviour is a compromise against natural rubber, so specify it for the oil, not for the ride.

Polychloroprene. Balanced across weather, ozone and moderate oil at once, which is what an exposed chassis or linkage bush actually faces. Slightly stiffer and less resilient than natural rubber, and worth the trade outdoors. Also the family we reach for when flame retardancy is specified.

Ethylene propylene diene rubber, the preferred material for weather-exposed linkages and anything near water, steam or coolant, with excellent ozone and UV resistance. Higher damping and lower resilience than natural rubber. Not for petroleum oils.
Styrene butadiene rubber. Abrasion resistance at low cost, blended with natural rubber where a bush takes rubbing contact rather than carrying a rate. Not for oil or fuel contact.

Fluorocarbon rubber, the first choice for aggressive chemical environments. High cost, high damping loss and low resilience, so it is rarely specified for a bush — it appears here because we mould it, and because a bush in a chemical or fuel environment occasionally needs it.

Vinyl methyl silicone, the widest service range of the eight. Poor tear and fatigue resistance, and a bonded part in silicone tends to fail at the bond line, so it is rarely specified for a bush — use it for a static high-temperature spacer rather than a loaded pivot.
fields.note: Eight panels. Natural rubber and AEM lead, which makes the accordion agree with the hero and the table for the first time. FKM and silicone move to last and each carries an explicit “rarely specified for a bush” clause — they stay visible because Margo moulds them, but an engineer needs to be told not to pick them for a loaded pivot. Every range matches the homepage compound table. The four live panels are rewritten rather than tuned: they describe chemical resistance, which is the wrong axis for this category
